\section{Introduction and Motivation}

The empirical study of economic relationships rests, almost without
exception, on some version of the regression model. Yet the
conditions under which regression yields reliable estimates of
structural parameters are considerably more stringent than is often
acknowledged in applied work. This section lays out the classical
framework, identifies the precise point at which it breaks down, and
sketches the remedies that the remainder of these notes develop in
full.


\subsection{The Classical Linear Model and Its Assumptions}


Let $\{(y_i, \bm{x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ be a sample of $n$ observations,
where $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$ is the dependent variable and
$\bm{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is a vector of regressors, with the
convention that its first component equals unity. The \emph{classical
linear model} (CLM) postulates

\begin{equation}
  y_i \;=\; \bm{x}_i^\top\,\bbeta_{0} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots,n,
  \label{eq:clm}
\end{equation}

\noindent where $\bbeta_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is the vector of true
parameters and $\varepsilon_i$ is an unobservable disturbance. Written
in matrix form, \eqref{eq:clm} becomes $\bY = \bX\bbeta_{0} + \beps$,
where $\bY \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $\bX \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}$, and
$\beps \in \mathbb{R}^n$ collect the observations in the obvious way.

\medskip

The ordinary least-squares (OLS) estimator is

\begin{equation}
  \hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}} \;=\;
  \bigl(\bX'\bX\bigr)^{-1}\bX'\bY \;=\;
  \bbeta_{0} + \bigl(\bX'\bX\bigr)^{-1}\bX'\beps.
  \label{eq:ols}
\end{equation}

Its desirable properties depend on the following assumptions, which
we state in a form suitable for asymptotic analysis.

\begin{assumption}[Linearity]
\label{ass:linearity}
The data-generating process satisfies \eqref{eq:clm} for some
$\bbeta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^k$.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Random Sampling]
\label{ass:sampling}
$\{(y_i, \bm{x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is an independent and identically
distributed (i.i.d.) sequence drawn from a well-defined population
distribution.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Full Rank]
\label{ass:rank}
$\E[\bm{x}_i \bm{x}_i^\top]$ is finite and positive definite, so that
$\rank(\bX'\bX) = k$ almost surely for $n$ sufficiently large.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Strict Exogeneity]
\label{ass:exogeneity}
$\E[\varepsilon_i \mid \bm{x}_i] = 0$ almost surely. As an immediate
consequence, $\E[\bm{x}_i \varepsilon_i] = \bm{0}$ and
$\E[\varepsilon_i] = 0$.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Spherical Disturbances]
\label{ass:spherical}
$\E[\varepsilon_i^2 \mid \bm{x}_i] = \sigma^2 \in (0,\infty)$ and
$\E[\varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j \mid \bm{x}_i, \bm{x}_j] = 0$ for all
$i \neq j$.
\end{assumption}

\begin{remark}
Assumption~\ref{ass:exogeneity} is the pivot around which the entire
analysis turns. It is substantially stronger than the \emph{mean
independence} condition $\E[\varepsilon_i \mid \bm{x}_i] = 0$; the
latter implies $\Cov(\bm{x}_i, \varepsilon_i) = \bm{0}$, but the
converse does not hold in general. The analysis below requires only
the zero-correlation form, $\E[\bm{x}_i \varepsilon_i] = \bm{0}$,
for consistency of OLS. We invoke the stronger form only where finite-
sample results are concerned.
\end{remark}

Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:linearity}--\ref{ass:exogeneity}, the
Gauss--Markov theorem establishes that OLS is the best linear
unbiased estimator (BLUE) of $\bbeta_0$. Consistency and asymptotic
normality follow from a standard application of the law of large
numbers and the central limit theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Consistency and Asymptotic Normality of OLS]
\label{thm:ols-can}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:linearity}--\ref{ass:exogeneity} and the
moment condition $\E\!\left[\norm{\bm{x}_i}^2 \varepsilon_i^2\right] 
\infty$,

\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}} \pto \bbeta_0$; and
  \item $\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}} - \bbeta_0\bigr)
        \dto \N\!\bigl(\bm{0},\, \bSigma_{\mathrm{OLS}}\bigr)$,
        where
        $\bSigma_{\mathrm{OLS}} =
         \bigl(\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)^{-1}
         \E\!\left[\varepsilon_i^2 \bm{x}_i \bm{x}_i^\top\right]
         \bigl(\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)^{-1}$.
\end{enumerate}
Under the additional Assumption~\ref{ass:spherical},
$\bSigma_{\mathrm{OLS}}$ simplifies to
$\sigma^2\bigl(\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
From \eqref{eq:ols},
$$
  \hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}} - \bbeta_0
  \;=\;
  \left(\frac{1}{n}\bX'\bX\right)^{-1}
  \frac{1}{n}\bX'\beps.
$$

By the LLN (Assumption~\ref{ass:sampling}),
$n^{-1}\bX'\bX \pto \E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]$, which is invertible by
Assumption~\ref{ass:rank}, and $n^{-1}\bX'\beps \pto
\E[\bm{x}_i\varepsilon_i] = \bm{0}$ by Assumption~\ref{ass:exogeneity}.
Part (i) follows from Slutsky's theorem. For part (ii), write
$n^{-1/2}\bX'\beps = n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n \bm{x}_i\varepsilon_i$.
The summands are i.i.d. with mean zero and covariance matrix
$\E[\varepsilon_i^2 \bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]$; the CLT yields
$n^{-1/2}\bX'\beps \dto \N\!\bigl(\bm{0},
\E[\varepsilon_i^2\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)$. The delta method (or
Slutsky) completes the argument.
\end{proof}


\subsection{Endogeneity: Definition, Sources, and Consequences}


The entire edifice of Theorem~\ref{thm:ols-can} collapses the moment
Assumption~\ref{ass:exogeneity} is violated.

\begin{definition}[Endogeneity]
\label{def:endogeneity}
A regressor $x_{ji}$ (the $j$-th component of $\bm{x}_i$) is said to
be \emph{endogenous} if $\Cov(x_{ji},\varepsilon_i) \neq 0$, or,
more generally, if $\E[\bm{x}_i\varepsilon_i] \neq \bm{0}$. The
model \eqref{eq:clm} is then said to suffer from \emph{endogeneity}.
\end{definition}

Endogeneity is not a single pathology but a family of related problems
sharing a common algebraic signature. We distinguish three principal
sources.

\subsubsection{Omitted Variable Bias}

Suppose the true model is
$$
  y_i \;=\; \bm{x}_i^\top\,\bbeta_0 + \gamma_0 c_i + u_i,
  \qquad \E[u_i \mid \bm{x}_i, c_i] = 0,
$$
where $c_i$ is an unobserved confounder correlated with $\bm{x}_i$.
If we estimate the misspecified model \eqref{eq:clm} with
$\varepsilon_i = \gamma_0 c_i + u_i$, then
$\E[\bm{x}_i \varepsilon_i] = \gamma_0 \E[\bm{x}_i c_i] \neq
\bm{0}$ whenever $\gamma_0 \neq 0$ and $c_i$ is correlated with at
least one regressor. This is the \emph{omitted variable bias} (OVB)
problem, arguably the most common form of endogeneity in applied
economics.

\subsubsection{Simultaneity Bias}

In many economic settings, $y_i$ and one or more components of
$\bm{x}_i$ are determined jointly by a system of equations. The
canonical example is a supply-and-demand system:
\begin{align*}
  q_i^d &= \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 p_i + \alpha_2 \bm{w}_i' \bm{\delta} + u_i^d
           \quad \text{(demand)}, \\
  q_i^s &= \beta_0  + \beta_1  p_i + \beta_2  \bm{r}_i' \bm{\phi}  + u_i^s
           \quad \text{(supply)}, \\
  q_i^d &= q_i^s
           \quad \text{(market clearing)}.
\end{align*}
In equilibrium, price $p_i$ is a function of both structural errors
$u_i^d$ and $u_i^s$. Regressing quantity on price therefore yields an
estimator that is inconsistent for either structural parameter.

\subsubsection{Measurement Error}

Let $x_i^*$ be the true value of a regressor, observed with error:
$x_i = x_i^* + v_i$, where $v_i$ is classical measurement error
with $\E[v_i] = 0$, $\Cov(x_i^*, v_i) = 0$. Substituting into the
true model $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i^* + u_i$ gives

$$
  y_i \;=\; \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \underbrace{(u_i - \beta_1 v_i)}_{=\,\varepsilon_i}.
$$

Since $\Cov(x_i, \varepsilon_i) = -\beta_1 \Var(v_i) \neq 0$, OLS
is inconsistent. The resulting \emph{attenuation bias} pushes the
estimate of $\beta_1$ toward zero in absolute value.

\medskip

The consequences of endogeneity are stark.

\begin{theorem}[Inconsistency of OLS under Endogeneity]
\label{thm:ols-inconsistent}
Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:exogeneity} fails, so that
$\bm{\delta} \equiv \E[\bm{x}_i\varepsilon_i] \neq \bm{0}$.
Then, under Assumptions~\ref{ass:linearity}--\ref{ass:rank},

$$
  \plim_{n\to\infty} \hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}
  \;=\;
  \bbeta_0 + \bigl(\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)^{-1}\bm{\delta}
  \;\neq\; \bbeta_0.
$$

Moreover, no amount of additional data can eliminate this
\emph{asymptotic bias}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the LLN applied to \eqref{eq:ols},
$$
  \plim\,\hat{\bbeta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}
  = \bbeta_0 +
  \left(\plim\,\frac{\bX'\bX}{n}\right)^{\!-1}
  \left(\plim\,\frac{\bX'\beps}{n}\right)
  = \bbeta_0 +
  \bigl(\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]\bigr)^{-1}\bm{\delta}.
$$
Because $\bm{\delta} \neq \bm{0}$ by hypothesis and
$\E[\bm{x}_i\bm{x}_i^\top]$ is non-singular by Assumption~\ref{ass:rank},
the second term is non-zero and persists as $n \to \infty$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:ols-inconsistent} makes clear that endogeneity is
fundamentally an identification problem, not a finite-sample one.
Collecting more data merely produces a more precise estimate of the
wrong quantity. The solution must address the source of the correlation
$\bm{\delta}$, not the sample size.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}[Returns to Schooling]
\label{ex:schooling}
Consider the classic Mincer earnings equation,
$$
  \log w_i \;=\; \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \bm{x}_i^\top\bgamma + \varepsilon_i,
$$
where $w_i$ is the wage, $S_i$ is years of schooling, and
$\bm{x}_i$ contains observable controls (age, region, etc.). The
parameter of interest, $\beta_1$, measures the average causal return
to an additional year of education. The problem is that $S_i$ is
almost certainly correlated with unobserved \emph{ability} $a_i$,
which also affects wages and is absorbed into $\varepsilon_i$. OLS
therefore overstates $\beta_1$. \citet{Card1993} addresses this by
instrumenting $S_i$ with proximity to a college, a variable that
plausibly affects schooling attainment without directly influencing
wages --- an application of the IV strategy introduced in
Section~\ref{sec:iv}.
\end{example}


\subsection{A Preview of Solutions}
\label{sec:preview}


Three broad strategies have been developed to recover consistent
estimates of $\bbeta_0$ in the presence of endogeneity. These notes
treat the first two in depth and briefly touch on their connections
to the third.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Instrumental Variables (IV).}\quad
The IV approach introduces a vector of \emph{instruments}
$\bm{z}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\ell}$ that satisfy two conditions:
\emph{relevance}, $\Cov(\bm{z}_i, \bm{x}_i) \neq \bm{0}$, and
\emph{exogeneity}, $\E[\bm{z}_i\varepsilon_i] = \bm{0}$. These two
conditions together restore identification. Section~\ref{sec:iv}
develops the IV estimator, establishes its asymptotic properties, and
discusses the critical practical issue of \emph{instrument strength}.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS).}\quad
When $\ell > k$ --- i.e.\ when there are more instruments than
endogenous regressors --- the model is \emph{overidentified} and IV
is no longer unique. 2SLS provides an optimal way to exploit all
available instruments simultaneously. Section~\ref{sec:tsls} derives
the 2SLS estimator, relates it to IV in the just-identified case, and
establishes its efficiency within the class of IV estimators under
homoskedastic errors.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Generalized Method of Moments (GMM).}\quad
GMM nests both IV and 2SLS as special cases. It begins from a set of
moment conditions $\E[\bm{g}(\bm{w}_i, \bbeta_0)] = \bm{0}$ and
constructs the estimator by minimising a quadratic form in the sample
analogue. With an \emph{optimal} weighting matrix, GMM achieves the
semiparametric efficiency bound within the class of estimators
exploiting the same moment conditions. Crucially, GMM extends to
heteroskedastic and autocorrelated errors without altering the
estimating equations --- a feature that makes it indispensable in
applied work. Section~\ref{sec:gmm} provides a self-contained
treatment.

\medskip

\noindent\textbf{Diagnostics.}\quad
Identifying endogeneity in a given dataset, assessing instrument
validity, and testing overidentifying restrictions are tasks of
independent importance. Section~\ref{sec:testing} covers the
Hausman test, the Sargan--Hansen $J$-statistic, and the
Stock--Yogo weak-instrument test.

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:intro1}
Consider the bivariate model $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i +
\varepsilon_i$ with $\Cov(x_i, \varepsilon_i) = \sigma_{x\varepsilon}
\neq 0$ and $\Var(x_i) = \sigma_x^2$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Show that $\plim\,\hat{\beta}_{1,\mathrm{OLS}} = \beta_1 +
        \sigma_{x\varepsilon}/\sigma_x^2$.
  \item Determine the sign of the asymptotic bias when (a) ability
        is the omitted variable in the schooling example, and (b)
        classical measurement error is present.
  \item Suppose you observe a variable $z_i$ with
        $\Cov(z_i, x_i) = \sigma_{zx} \neq 0$ and
        $\Cov(z_i, \varepsilon_i) = 0$. Propose an estimator for
        $\beta_1$ based on these covariances, and verify that it is
        consistent.
\end{enumerate}
\end{exercise}
